Special Background Courses are core academic components designed to support the field of Electrical and Electronic Engineering in areas such as the study and construction of systems for the generation, transmission, distribution, storage, processing, control, and utilization of energy and information, as well as computing and communications. The courses include subjects such as signals and systems, logic circuit design, digital systems design, computer systems architecture, analog electronics, electromagnetic fields, automatic control, electric machines, telecommunications, and power electronics.

In the second specialization semester for Cycle C, students take three required courses and three compulsory electives selected from six subjects, reaching 30 ECTS.

The program emphasizes both theoretical instruction and practical application. Students engage in laboratory work, projects, and internships that prepare them for real-world engineering challenges. They learn to troubleshoot technical issues, design innovative solutions, and work with cutting-edge technologies. This hands-on approach ensures that graduates are ready to contribute effectively to their fields upon entering the workforce.

Graduates are equipped with both theoretical and practical knowledge across a broad range of subjects in electrical and electronic engineering. Their education provides them with the necessary orientation to meet market demands efficiently. They gain the ability to analyze and process problems, select the most appropriate methods for solving them, utilize modern information and communication technologies, and evaluate the outcomes of their proposed solutions. Additionally, they are trained to work effectively both individually and as part of a team.

Each study cycle provides students with a structured combination of mandatory and elective courses. This allows them to gain deeper knowledge in their chosen area while having some flexibility to shape their curriculum according to interests and career goals.

The Administrative Personnel ensures the smooth operation of the department by handling paperwork, managing student records, assisting faculty with academic procedures, and coordinating department activities. They provide essential support to both students and staff, ensuring that academic and administrative processes run efficiently.

Laboratory components must be attended sufficiently for a course grade to be recorded. Sufficient attendance requires at least 80% presence in conducted lab exercises, submission of the required written reports and assignments, and participation in all scheduled assessment activities for those exercises. If a final lab examination is provided, students must take it regardless of performance during the semester.

Courses that have both a theoretical and a laboratory component are treated as a single, unified course. The final grade is computed as a weighted average of the theoretical and laboratory parts as defined in the course syllabus, provided the laboratory attendance requirements are met. If the laboratory part has not been sufficiently attended, no course grade is recorded, regardless of the theoretical performance. Failure in either part entails retaking the course according to the syllabus rules.

Students become eligible to undertake the Diploma Thesis during the ninth (9th) semester of studies. There is no formal limit on the number of outstanding courses at the time of assignment, but it is recommended that students first succeed in at least 45 of the 55 courses required for graduation. Students choose a topic in agreement with a faculty member and submit an application to the Department Secretariat. At the start of each semester, the student must enroll in the 'Diploma Thesis' course. Semesters officially suspended under current legislation do not count toward any maximum time limits. Completion occurs when the supervisor confirms that the agreed objectives have been satisfactorily achieved in scope, depth, results, and document quality.

The Diploma Supplement is an explanatory document issued together with the degree. It describes the nature, level, educational framework, content, and status of the studies. It does not replace the original degree, nor does it constitute automatic recognition or an equivalence statement. Its purpose is to make the qualification easier to understand, especially outside the country of issue.

Courses and instructors are evaluated electronically by students during the 8th to 12th teaching weeks of each semester. The Department’s Internal Evaluation Group (OM.E.A.) organizes the online evaluation process to maximize participation. After the evaluation period ends, OM.E.A. studies the results and submits written improvement proposals to the Department Assembly, and a summary extract is sent to the University’s Quality Assurance Unit (MODIP) within about one month of the Assembly meeting.

Program rules distinguish compulsory, compulsory‑elective (specialized) and optional courses; foreign‑language requirements are listed in the Diploma Supplement.
The undergraduate program comprises ten academic semesters. The first nine semesters are devoted to coursework, and the tenth semester is dedicated to the Diploma Thesis.

Students must renew their registration and submit a semester course declaration within the official deadlines announced in the academic calendar and on the Department website. The procedure is electronic via the Student Information portal (e‑secretariat). If a student misses the declaration window, they may, within ten (10) calendar days, file a justified late‑registration request with the Department Secretariat, listing the courses to be attended. Requests are accepted only if the reasons are adequately justified.

The e‑secretariat is the online student information system used for registration and re‑registration, semester course declarations, grade viewing, and obtaining electronic certificates such as enrollment statements.

Assessment methods are defined in each course’s official syllabus and can include written examinations, oral examinations, laboratory evaluations, projects, and individual or group assignments. The syllabus states the exact components, their weight in the final grade, and any permitted materials or special conditions (e.g., open‑book rules, calculator use). Continuous assessment (midterms, quizzes, presentations, graded homework) may be used. When a laboratory component exists, its rules and deliverables are binding and contribute as specified. Retake examinations are conducted only within the official examination windows set by the academic calendar; ad‑hoc make‑ups are not normally offered.

Teaching weeks and examination windows are distinct periods. Final examinations take place solely within the official exam sessions. Students must bring valid identification, arrive on time, follow seating instructions, and observe the materials policy stated by the syllabus or invigilators. Electronic devices are restricted unless explicitly permitted. Invigilators may check identity and seating at any time, and academic integrity applies to all assessments. Detailed timetables (date, room, duration) are announced in advance through departmental postings and the student portal; any retake conditions are published with the exam schedule.

Registration (re‑registration) and the semester course declaration are completed electronically via the student portal (e‑secretariat) during the published window. Students select courses within the allowable study load and confirm their choices; a confirmation receipt is available in the portal. If the declaration window is missed, a justified late‑registration request may be submitted to the Department Secretariat within ten (10) calendar days after the deadline. Approval is not automatic and depends on adequate justification and capacity constraints. Declaration deadlines align with the academic calendar, and the portal shows status (pending/submitted/confirmed) and current registrations; edits are allowed while the window remains open.

Through the e‑secretariat, students can request official electronic certificates, such as enrollment statements and grade/transcript documents. Requests require authentication with institutional credentials and can be tracked in the portal until they are processed and available for download. Issued documents include institutional validation (e.g., digital signature or verification code) suitable for third‑party verification where accepted. Availability, languages (e.g., English where offered), processing times, and any fees are indicated in the posted procedures. Previously issued files remain accessible for re‑download.

The internship (practical training) enables students to apply academic knowledge in real professional environments under academic supervision. Departmental calls describe eligibility, duration, timing, host selection, supervision arrangements, deadlines, deliverables, and any funding or insurance terms. Successful completion typically requires performing assigned tasks at the host organization, adhering to safety and conduct rules, and submitting a final report and any additional deliverables specified by the department. Evaluation combines the host’s feedback with academic review; where used, a learning agreement clarifies objectives and outputs.

Diploma Thesis work is carried out under the supervision of a faculty member once eligibility begins (normally from the ninth semester). It is recommended—though not strictly required—that students have already succeeded in most of their courses (e.g., on the order of 45 out of 55) before starting. The topic is agreed with the supervisor, an application is filed with the Department Secretariat, and students must enroll in the ‘Diploma Thesis’ course each semester while the thesis is in progress. Semesters officially suspended do not count toward time limits. Completion is confirmed when the supervisor judges that agreed objectives have been met in scope, depth, results, and document quality; formatting, submission, and any presentation/defense requirements are communicated in departmental instructions.

The degree is awarded once all program requirements and obligations have been completed and recorded by the Department and central services. Graduation procedures—including any application step, issuance of degree documents, and ceremony logistics—are announced through official channels. A Diploma Supplement is issued together with the degree to explain the nature, level, framework, content, and status of the qualification; it is not an equivalence or automatic recognition statement. Students may request additional certified copies according to institutional procedures; any fees or language options (e.g., English) are indicated in the instructions.

Mobility and recognition (e.g., ERASMUS) follow ECTS principles and a pre‑approved learning agreement signed by the student, the home department, and the host institution. After mobility, the host transcript is matched to the agreement, and the Department considers content, learning outcomes, and workload to determine equivalence and transfer of credits. Recognition may be full or partial depending on the match; grade conversions are applied where required by institutional policy. Deadlines and application steps are published by International Relations and the Department.

Courses with theory and lab form a unified course with syllabus‑defined weighting. Student course evaluations are conducted online during teaching weeks 8–12; results inform departmental improvements. Electronic services (e‑secretariat) are used for registrations, declarations, grades, and certificates; students are responsible for monitoring official notices and meeting deadlines.

Retake examinations take place only within the official exam sessions defined in the academic calendar. Ad‑hoc make‑ups are not normally offered. Any exceptions or special arrangements are communicated through official announcements and must be followed exactly.

Detailed exam timetables are published in advance and include dates, rooms, and duration. Last‑minute changes can occur; students should check the portal and official notices on the day of the exam and follow invigilators’ directions on seating and timing.

During exams, students must comply with invigilators, maintain silence, and keep only approved materials on the desk. Identity and seating may be checked at any time. Breaches of conduct or integrity are handled under the institution’s disciplinary procedures and may void the exam.

Assessment may combine a final exam with continuous components such as midterms, quizzes, presentations, projects, or lab work. Weights, permitted materials, and any special conditions are set in the syllabus or exam announcement and apply to both theory and laboratory parts where relevant.

Exam conditions are set by the Department and the course syllabus. Permitted materials are explicitly stated; anything not listed is not allowed. Electronic devices are restricted unless explicitly permitted. Academic integrity applies to all assessments; unauthorized aids or communication may invalidate results.

Approved exam accommodations are arranged in advance according to posted procedures. Arrangements may affect seating, timing, or permitted materials as authorized. Students are responsible for submitting documentation early enough for scheduling.

For courses with laboratory or practical components, assessment rules for the lab part are binding. The final grade reflects the components and weights defined for theory and lab. Where specified, lab sufficiency rules (attendance, required submissions) apply to sit the final exam.

Campus network services include Wi‑Fi and (where offered) VPN for remote access. Connection requires institutional credentials and adherence to acceptable‑use rules. Configuration instructions are published by IT; device security is the student’s responsibility.

The learning management system (LMS) hosts course materials, announcements, and online assessments. Enrollment in LMS spaces follows course registrations in the portal. If a course is missing after registration, students should check again after synchronization or contact support.

Password resets are performed through the official login recovery flow using institutional identifiers. If recovery options fail or access is locked, support can re‑enable the account after identity verification. Students should update recovery methods once access is restored.

Account security and data protection policies apply to all IT services. Students must not share passwords or access others’ accounts. Suspected compromise should be reported immediately so credentials can be reset and sessions revoked.

Institutional IT accounts are issued to enrolled students for access to the portal, email, Wi‑Fi, and learning systems. Activation uses the identifiers provided at enrollment and must follow the posted steps. Students are responsible for safeguarding credentials and updating contact details in the portal.

Lost or damaged student ID cards can be replaced by following the posted replacement procedure. Students should report loss promptly, request a new card through the portal or Secretariat as instructed, and bring valid identification when collecting the replacement.

Where multi‑factor authentication (MFA) is enabled, students must enroll a second factor and keep it updated. Recovery procedures are available through support if the second factor is lost. MFA helps protect access to email and other sensitive services.

IT and student‑services support is available through published channels, such as helpdesk tickets, email, or Secretariat office hours. Requests should include institutional ID and a clear description of the issue; official responses are provided via the portal or email.

An institutional email account is provided for official communications. Students should monitor it regularly, as deadlines and announcements are sent there. Mailbox settings, forwarding, and name formats follow institutional conventions; misuse may result in restriction.

Remote or hybrid arrangements are possible where the host and Department allow them. Approval depends on the nature of tasks, supervision arrangements, and the ability to verify outcomes and attendance.
Changes to placement terms or cancellations require approval and must follow posted procedures. Unilateral withdrawal or no‑show can affect recognition and eligibility for future calls.

Eligibility, timing within the study plan, and any prerequisites are specified in official announcements. Students should plan early, as placements may be competitive and require coordination with coursework. Where a learning agreement is used, objectives and tasks are approved in advance.

Departmental calls describe eligibility, timing, duration, host selection, supervision, deadlines, required deliverables, and any funding or insurance terms. Work must follow host policies and academic instructions.
Internship schedules should not conflict with academic obligations. Students must coordinate hours with the host and supervisor so that required coursework and exams can be completed without overlap.

Internship participation must comply with legal, safety, and data‑protection obligations. Any required insurance or agreements are indicated in the call or procedures. Students must follow workplace rules, confidentiality, and any security clearances required by the host.

Applications follow the published call, including required documents and deadlines. Selection may consider academic progress, fit with host tasks, and capacity limits. Applicants are notified through official channels and must accept offers within the stated timeframe.

An academic supervisor oversees learning objectives and progress. Successful completion typically requires performing assigned tasks at the host and submitting a final report or other deliverables. Evaluation combines host feedback with academic review according to departmental criteria.

Deliverables are stated in the call or instructions and may include a final report, logbook, presentation, or supervisor sign‑offs. Submission methods and deadlines are announced; late or incomplete submissions can delay evaluation and credit award.

Host organizations may include companies, public bodies, research units, or laboratories. Placement aims to match tasks with the student’s study area and learning objectives; availability depends on hosts’ capacity and cycles.

Internships carry credits according to program rules and ECTS principles. Recognition is based on verified completion of tasks and deliverables aligned with the approved objectives. Where applicable, equivalence from prior documented experience is considered under departmental policy.
Students should keep payment confirmations and receipts. Where supported, the portal stores a history of completed requests including downloadable files and status logs suitable for later reference.

Replacement of lost or damaged student identification cards may involve a fee where applicable. The replacement procedure requires prompt reporting, identity verification, and following the payment and collection steps as posted.

Where administrative policy applies, unresolved payments can result in temporary holds on certain services until cleared. Students should retain receipts and monitor the portal to confirm that holds are lifted after payment is registered.

Refunds or corrections are handled according to the published policy. Requests should include the receipt/transaction reference and a brief explanation. Approval depends on timing and the state of processing at the time the issue is reported.

Payment methods and instructions—such as electronic payments or deposits where applicable—are specified in the request flow or the published procedure. Students should follow the exact reference codes and keep the receipt or confirmation for verification.
If a service defines late penalties or re‑processing charges, these are described in its specific instructions. Students should observe the stated window to avoid extra cost and processing delays.

Deadlines for fee‑bearing requests align with administrative calendars and are announced with each service. Processing begins after the request and, where applicable, payment confirmation. Students should monitor the portal or email for status updates and pick‑up or download instructions.

Where waivers or reduced fees are applicable (for example, defined categories or programs), they are stated in the published conditions. Students must submit any required proof during the request so eligibility can be verified before processing.

Official certificates and transcripts are requested through the portal. Electronic documents are typically issued with validation; where printed certified copies are requested, fees and pickup instructions—if any—are indicated in the procedure.

Some administrative services may include fees, as indicated in the posted procedures or during the online request flow. Examples can include certified copies, special reprints, or replacements. Payment instructions, amounts (if any), and processing times are communicated in the official announcement or portal steps.

Issuance of additional certified degree documents or supplements can carry a fee where specified. The request flow outlines identity verification, payment method, and when documents are ready for collection or download.

Approved accommodations for coursework can include alternative formats, adjusted deadlines for disability‑related reasons, or accessible lab setups. Instructors apply the authorized adjustments while maintaining essential learning outcomes and academic standards.

Short‑term injuries or health conditions may warrant temporary academic adjustments. Students submit the request with relevant documentation; eligibility and duration are determined case‑by‑case under the procedure.

Students who need accommodations register through the published disability support procedure. Requests should be made early so arrangements can be scheduled before teaching and examinations. The process explains documentation requirements, timelines, and how approved accommodations are communicated to instructors.

Documentation requirements are stated in the procedure. Medical or diagnostic information is handled confidentially and used only to determine functional needs. Staff communicate approved accommodations—not diagnoses—to instructors, and records are stored according to data‑protection rules.

Exam accommodations (e.g., extra time, separate room, assistive technology) are arranged in advance. Students should submit requests by the stated deadline so rooming, invigilation, and technology can be scheduled. Invigilators apply the approved conditions exactly as authorized.

For physical access needs, students can request classroom relocations, reserved seating, or other arrangements. Emergency evacuation planning is coordinated with the relevant offices to ensure safe egress for students with mobility or sensory needs.

Accessible materials (e.g., large print, searchable PDFs, captions) and assistive‑technology support are provided where authorized. Students should request conversions early, as processing time may be needed for captioning or format changes.

Instructors receive only the accommodation plan necessary to implement adjustments. Students are not required to disclose diagnoses to instructors; the disability support office manages documentation and privacy.

Where a disability affects participation in a particular assessment format, an alternative method may be authorized if it preserves the course’s essential outcomes. Decisions are coordinated by the disability support office with the instructor.

If a student believes an approved accommodation was not implemented or was wrongly denied, they may use the published grievance or appeal route. The process specifies how to submit concerns and expected response timelines.

Where applicable, service animals and approved support arrangements are accommodated consistent with policy and law. Handlers must maintain control and follow campus rules; questions about access should be directed to the disability support office.

If disability‑related adjustments are needed for housing or dining, students follow the posted request process and submit documentation. Eligibility, available options, and timelines are communicated in the respective procedures.

Once accommodations are approved, instructors are notified of the authorized measures. Students should discuss any course‑specific logistics (labs, fieldwork, presentations) early to ensure timely implementation.

Interpreting or real‑time captioning services are arranged where authorized. Lead time is required to schedule providers; students should submit detailed timetables as early as possible so coverage can be arranged.

Accommodations are not normally retroactive. Requests should be filed before assessments so scheduling and resources can be arranged. If circumstances change suddenly, students should contact support immediately to explore timely options.

If assistive technology fails during an assessment, students should inform the invigilator immediately and contact support so the issue can be addressed. Contingency steps are handled under the exam accommodations procedure.
